warmup.q: A program has been running for an hour. An agent attaches and changes the body of SoundBoard.play(). A SoundBoard object created at start-up calls play() again. Which body runs?
options: The old one: objects keep the class version they were created with
The new one: the class changed in place, and the old object uses the same class
Neither: the call throws because the class changed
The new one, but only after a restart
warmup.why: Retransformation replaces method bodies inside the existing Class object, and objects don't carry their own copy of the code, so the next call on the old object runs the new body. Only a call that was already running when the change happened finishes on the old bytecode. No restart is involved. The second section shows it on a live object.

opening:
A touring show uses the same prompt book every night. Say the stage manager wants each lighting cue timed. Nobody rewrites the script or hires a stand-in for each actor. The stage manager can slip a note into the prompt book before rehearsal starts: "start a stopwatch here". In an emergency, they can walk in mid-performance and paste a correction over one page.

The JVM lets a Java agent do both. An agent is a small program that holds a key to every class the JVM loads. It sees each class's bytes as they load, and it can rewrite a class that's already running. The last lesson's ClassFile API only made new classes. Monitoring tools, which record how long each part of a program takes, use agents to change classes you never wrote.

Agents are easy to misjudge both ways. People expect them to need a restart, and they don't. People expect them to change anything, and they can't. In this lesson, we'll write a startup agent, change a class under a live object, read the warning JDK 21 added, and let Byte Buddy write the change. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a stage manager who slips a note into the prompt book before rehearsal, or pastes a correction over a page mid-run. An agent does both: a transformer sees each class as it loads, and retransformation swaps method bodies under live objects, never the class's shape. That ends this track, from props fetched on first use to prompt books edited mid-show.

Now run your tests without -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading and search the output for loaded dynamically. Each hit names a jar that will need the flag, or -javaagent.

Next, we'll start the track on memory and garbage collection. Every class we loaded and every object made from it lives somewhere. Where, and what does each object carry besides its fields?

sections.h: Before rehearsal: a startup agent watches every class load
sections.html:
Lessons 4 and 5 added work by wrapping objects. That needs an interface or a class that isn't final, and it misses self-calls whenever the proxy forwards. It also only works on objects that were created through the proxy. Sometimes you need more: timing a method inside a library jar, or tracing a class that a framework creates for you. A Java agent works on the class instead of the object.

An agent is an ordinary class with a special entry point. The JVM calls it with a java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation, the JDK's handle for watching and changing classes: the stage manager's key. There are three ways to start one:

  • java -javaagent:agent.jar[=args] calls the agent's premain(String args, Instrumentation inst) before your main. You can repeat the option, and the agents start in the order you list them.
  • An executable jar can name an agent in its manifest with Launcher-Agent-Class. The JVM calls that agent's agentmain before the application's main.
  • A tool can attach to a JVM that is already running and load an agent jar into it. The JVM then calls agentmain(String, Instrumentation). The third section is about this case.

The manifest is a small text file inside a jar, META-INF/MANIFEST.MF, that describes the jar. An agent jar's manifest names the agent class with Premain-Class or Agent-Class, and Can-Retransform-Classes: true asks for the right to change classes that are already loaded.

The first thing most agents do is register a ClassFileTransformer. From then on, the JVM calls its transform method with the bytes of every class it is about to define. The method returns new bytes, or null, which means "no change". The smallest useful agent changes nothing and only watches:

Java
public static void premain(String args, Instrumentation inst) {
    inst.addTransformer(new ClassFileTransformer() {
        @Override
        public byte[] transform(ClassLoader loader, String className, Class<?> redefined,
                                ProtectionDomain domain, byte[] bytes) {
            System.out.println("[agent] loading " + className + " (" + bytes.length + " bytes)");
            return null;                                   // null: leave the class as it is
        }
    });
}
Kotlin
@JvmStatic
fun premain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) {
    inst.addTransformer(object : ClassFileTransformer {
        override fun transform(
            loader: ClassLoader?, className: String?, redefined: Class<*>?,
            domain: ProtectionDomain?, bytes: ByteArray,
        ): ByteArray? {
            println("[agent] loading $className (${bytes.size} bytes)")
            return null                                    // null: leave the class as it is
        }
    })
}

The bytes that transform receives are the class files of lesson 6. An agent that wants to change a class rewrites them, with the ClassFile API on JDK 24 and later, or with a library such as Byte Buddy. Notice that the transformer above is an anonymous class, not a lambda. Both of ClassFileTransformer's transform methods are default methods, so it isn't a functional interface.

This section's demo builds an agent jar that holds only a manifest, then starts a second JVM with -javaagent:<jar>=opening-night. On JDK 25 it printed:

[agent] premain args=opening-night, classes already loaded: 890
[agent] loading workbench/bytecode/l07/AgentTarget (1376 bytes)
main: started
[agent] loading workbench/bytecode/l07/AgentTarget$Ticket (1667 bytes)
main: Ticket[show=Hamlet, seat=B12]
[agent] transformer saw 30 class definitions

premain ran first, when 890 JDK classes had already loaded. The agent saw AgentTarget before main started, and its Ticket record just before its first use: the lazy loading of lesson 1. That's the note slipped in before rehearsal. Nearly every class of your application loads after premain returns, so a startup agent sees almost all of them. And no warning appeared, because an agent named on the command line is on the guest list.

A transformer sees each class once, as the JVM defines it. Register it before the classes you care about load.

But what about a class that loaded an hour ago?

Then the agent reports AgentTarget, then main: started, then AgentTarget$Ticket just before it's used, then main: Ticket[show=Hamlet, seat=B12]. At exit, transformer saw N class definitions, a few dozen, because a record's first use also loads some JDK support classes. The Kotlin twin reports KAgentTarget and KTicket. No warning appears: an agent named on the command line is not a dynamic load.

video.title: A Java agent's transformer sees each class's bytes as the JVM defines it; retransformation swaps method bodies in a class already loaded

sections.h: During the run: retransformation swaps method bodies under live objects
sections.html:
An agent that arrives late doesn't need a restart, at least for method bodies. Instrumentation.retransformClasses(classes...) runs the registered transformers again on classes that are already loaded, and installs the result in place. The Class object stays the same, so every existing object and every reference to the class sees the new code. It's the correction pasted over one page of the prompt book: the next actor who reaches that cue reads the new version.

This section's demo does it to a final class, StageClock, whose now() returns "tick". It creates a clock, attaches an agent to its own JVM, and adds timing code to now(). With its warning lines left out (they're the next section's subject), it printed this on JDK 21:

before: tick
retransform supported: true
  [advice] workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo$StageClock.now took 14176 ns
after:  tick   (the same object, no restart)

The same clock, created before the agent existed, ran the new body on its next call. It still says tick; only now someone is timing it. Its class is final, so no subclass proxy from lesson 5 could have touched it.

The Instrumentation Javadoc lists what that does and doesn't mean:

  • "If a retransformed method has active stack frames, those active frames continue to run the bytecodes of the original method. The retransformed method will be used on new invokes."
  • "Redefining a class does not cause its initializers to be run. The values of static variables will remain as they were."
  • "If this method throws an exception, no classes have been retransformed."

An active stack frame is a call that is still running. So an actor in mid-line finishes the line from the old page, and the next actor reads the new one. And lesson 1's dress rehearsal, <clinit>, isn't held again.

There's a hard limit on what may change. JVMTI, the JVM Tool Interface, is the native interface that debuggers and agents are built on, and it says: "The retransformation must not add, remove or rename fields or methods, change the signatures of methods, change modifiers, or change inheritance." Method bodies, the constant pool and attributes may change. You can rewrite what a cue says, but you can't add a character to the cast list. So an agent can add timing code to now(), but it can't add a long calls field to count with. The count must live somewhere else, such as a public class that the new code calls. That's what the lab's CallCounts is for.

The same limit explains the other direction. A transformer that wants to add members can only do so when the class is first loaded. That means registering it before the class loads, usually through -javaagent.

Retransformation also needs permission. The agent's manifest must say Can-Retransform-Classes: true, and each transformer that should run again must be registered with addTransformer(transformer, true). isRetransformClassesSupported() reports whether this JVM and agent allow it, and it printed true above.

Here the prompt-book picture breaks. In a theatre, a correction pasted into one prompt book changes one copy. A class exists once per class loader, so one retransformation changes the code for every object of that class, and for every caller, at once.

Retransformation swaps method bodies in place, for every caller at once. It never changes the class's shape.

The demo printed four lines of warning before it got that far. The JVM printed them because this agent arrived late.

try.title: Change a class under a live object
steps: Read LiveRetransformDemo (or the Kotlin twin). StageClock is final, and KStageClock is final because it's Kotlin.
Before running it: will the after: call on the same clock print an advice line? Will you see a warning?
Run it with the command below and read the output from top to bottom.

code.title: LiveRetransformDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l07; import net.bytebuddy.agent.ByteBuddyAgent; import net.bytebuddy.agent.builder.AgentBuilder; import net.bytebuddy.asm.Advice; import java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.is; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** Attach an agent to this running JVM and change a loaded class under a live object. */ public class LiveRetransformDemo { public static final class StageClock { // final: lesson 5's subclass proxies couldn't touch it public String now() { return "tick"; } } public static class TimingAdvice { @Advice.OnMethodEnter static long enter() { return System.nanoTime(); // copied to the start of now() } @Advice.OnMethodExit(onThrowable = Throwable.class) static void exit(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") String where, @Advice.Enter long t0) { System.out.println(" [advice] " + where + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) + " ns"); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0) { // -Pargs=allowed or -Pargs=blocked relaunch(args[0]); return; } StageClock clock = new StageClock(); System.out.println("before: " + clock.now()); Instrumentation inst = ByteBuddyAgent.install(); // self-attach: JEP 451 warns unless allowed System.out.println("retransform supported: " + inst.isRetransformClassesSupported()); new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(is(StageClock.class)) .transform((builder, type, loader, module, domain) -> builder.visit(Advice.to(TimingAdvice.class).on(named("now")))) .installOn(inst); System.out.println("after: " + clock.now() + " (the same object, no restart)"); } /** Runs this demo again in a child JVM with dynamic agent loading explicitly allowed or blocked. */ static void relaunch(String mode) throws Exception { String flag = mode.equals("blocked") ? "-XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading" : "-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading"; String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), LiveRetransformDemo.class.getName()) .redirectErrorStream(true) .start(); System.out.println("child JVM with " + flag + ":"); child.getInputStream().transferTo(System.out); System.out.println("child exited with " + child.waitFor()); } }

Then comes [advice] ...StageClock.now took ... ns, printed from inside now(), and after: tick (the same object, no restart). The object was created before the agent existed, its class is final, and nothing was restarted.

sections.h: Arriving mid-run: the warning JDK 21 prints, and the flag behind it
sections.html:
The four lines come from JEP 451, "Prepare to Disallow the Dynamic Loading of Agents", which was delivered in JDK 21:

WARNING: A Java agent has been loaded dynamically (.../byte-buddy-agent-1.18.17.jar)
WARNING: If a serviceability tool is in use, please run with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading to hide this warning
WARNING: If a serviceability tool is not in use, please run with -Djdk.instrument.traceUsage for more information
WARNING: Dynamic loading of agents will be disallowed by default in a future release

Picture a security desk at the stage door that logs anyone who arrives during a performance with a key. A dynamic load is any agent that arrives after start-up, through the attach mechanism, the JDK's way for one program to connect to a JVM that is already running. ByteBuddyAgent.install() attaches to its own JVM, and so does any library that self-attaches. A serviceability tool, in the warning's words, is a tool for watching or fixing a running program, such as a profiler or a debugger. The java.lang.instrument documentation says "the JVM prints a warning on the standard error stream for each agent that it attempts to start in a running JVM".

The documentation also names the switch for HotSpot, the JVM in the usual OpenJDK builds. -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading opts in and hides the warning. -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading refuses the load, and then ByteBuddyAgent.install() throws IllegalStateException: Could not self-attach to current VM using external process. An agent started with -javaagent never warns: the startup demo printed nothing of the kind.

Today the default is still "allow, with a warning". In the jdk-25-ga source, the flag is declared product(bool, EnableDynamicAgentLoading, true, ...). Runs for this track on JDK 21, 25, 26 and 27.0.1 all warned and then loaded the agent. The last line says the default will change. When it does, every tool and test that self-attaches without the flag will fail at start-up.

So decide on purpose. If a program needs an agent in production, start it with -javaagent, so it's there from the first class. If a test suite self-attaches, add the flag to the test JVM. The labs' Gradle build passes -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading to every test task, which is why the lab runs quietly. To find what would break, run your tests once without the flag and search the output for the warning.

On JDK 25, the demo printed four more lines, and they're a different warning:

WARNING: A terminally deprecated method in sun.misc.Unsafe has been called
WARNING: sun.misc.Unsafe::objectFieldOffset has been called by net.bytebuddy.dynamic.loading.ClassInjector$UsingUnsafe$Dispatcher$CreationAction (...)
WARNING: Please consider reporting this to the maintainers of class net.bytebuddy.dynamic.loading.ClassInjector$UsingUnsafe$Dispatcher$CreationAction
WARNING: sun.misc.Unsafe::objectFieldOffset will be removed in a future release

The security desk has a colleague. These lines come from JEP 498. From JDK 24, the JDK warns by default when code uses the memory-access methods of sun.misc.Unsafe, an old internal class for raw memory access. Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder triggered it. Byte Buddy's release notes show it moving away from Unsafe (1.18.10: "Delay change of default for unsafe use to Java 26"), and in the research runs for this track, JDK 26 and 27 printed no such lines.

A late agent works today, with a warning, and will be refused later. Start agents with -javaagent, or allow late ones on purpose.

Whichever way the agent arrives, writing its changes by hand is still the hard part.

aside.title: Which agents are already in my programs?
aside.html: Probably more than you think. Monitoring and tracing tools, which record how long each request takes, usually arrive with -javaagent at start-up, so they never warn. Some mocking libraries, which build stand-in objects for tests, attach an agent to the test JVM on their own, and on JDK 21 and later that prints the JEP 451 warning in your test output. Profilers and debuggers that you attach by hand to a running program load agents too. Run your tests once without -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading and read the warnings: each one names the jar that attached.

sections.h: Writing the note with Byte Buddy: AgentBuilder and Advice
sections.html:
Writing a ClassFileTransformer that edits bytecode by hand means parsing the class, changing it and writing it out again, with lesson 6's tools. Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder does the plumbing, and its Advice does the editing. The lab's SoundBoard is a final Kotlin class whose play(cue) plays one sound cue. This is the lab's solution, which counts every call to play:

Java
ResettableClassFileTransformer t = new AgentBuilder.Default()
        .disableClassFormatChanges()                              // 1. no new members: required to retransform
        .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) // 2. also rewrite classes already loaded
        .type(is(SoundBoard.class))                               // 3. which classes
        .transform((builder, type, loader, module, domain) ->
                builder.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice.class).on(named("play"))))  // 4. what to change
        .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install());                     // 5. attach, register, retransform now
Kotlin
val t = AgentBuilder.Default()
    .disableClassFormatChanges()                                  // 1. no new members: required to retransform
    .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION)     // 2. also rewrite classes already loaded
    .type(`is`(SoundBoard::class.java))                           // 3. which classes
    .transform { builder, _, _, _, _ ->
        builder.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice::class.java).on(named("play")))  // 4. what to change
    }
    .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install())                          // 5. attach, register, retransform now

Read it in order. disableClassFormatChanges() promises not to add members, which retransformation requires. RETRANSFORMATION asks Byte Buddy to rewrite matching classes that are already loaded, not only new ones. type(...) picks the classes, and transform says what to change in them. Last, installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()) attaches the agent, registers the transformer and retransforms at once.

By default, Advice doesn't call your code at all. Byte Buddy copies the body of your @Advice.OnMethodEnter method into the start of the target method, and the body of an @Advice.OnMethodExit method into every exit. It's the stage manager's note written onto the page itself, not a messenger standing next to it. That's why advice methods must be static, and why they may only call public code: the copied code runs inside the target class. It's also why @Advice.Origin("#t.#m") can hand them the method's name as a constant.

Nothing new is added to the class, so the result keeps to the retransformation rule. Lesson 5's MethodDelegation adds accessor methods and helper classes, so it only works on new classes, or on classes that aren't loaded yet. The transformer that installOn returns has a reset(inst, RETRANSFORMATION) method, which puts the original bodies back.

Because the advice runs inside the method, it sees every call, from anywhere: from other classes, from the class itself through this, and on final classes. Here are the track's three ways to intercept a call, side by side:

needs this.method() calls final classes and methods
JDK proxy (lesson 4) an interface not seen not relevant
subclass proxy (lesson 5) an open class seen only if the proxy is the object can't intercept
agent with Advice an agent seen fine

Advice copies your code into the method itself, so it sees every call. Keep it static, and call only public code from it.

The price is reach, and it's this tool's limit. An agent can rewrite any method body, but never the shape of a class that is already loaded. Every rewrite lands on every caller in that class loader at once, and loading the agent late earns a warning. Use a proxy when you own the call path, and an agent when you must change code you don't control.

Check yourself before the lab: SoundBoard.playAll calls play three times on this. With the advice installed on play, how many calls does CallCounts record when you call playAll once? (Three. Each inner call runs play's new body, which begins with the copied advice.)

compare.title: The counting advice in Java and Kotlin

java.title: CountingAdvice.java
java.html: public class CountingAdvice { @Advice.OnMethodEnter // copied to the start of the method static void enter(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") String method) { CallCounts.hit(method); // must be public: this code runs in the target class } } // install it new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(is(SoundBoard.class)) .transform((b, type, loader, module, domain) -> b.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice.class).on(named("play")))) .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install());

kotlin.title: CountingAdvice.kt
kotlin.html: object CountingAdvice { @JvmStatic // Advice needs a real static method @Advice.OnMethodEnter // copied to the start of the method fun enter(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") method: String) { CallCounts.hit(method) // must be public: this code runs in the target class } } // install it AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(`is`(SoundBoard::class.java)) .transform { b, _, _, _, _ -> b.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice::class.java).on(named("play"))) } .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install())

compare.note: Kotlin has no static, so the advice lives in an object with @JvmStatic, which makes kotlinc write a real static method that Byte Buddy can copy. is is a Kotlin keyword, so the matcher must be written `is`(...). The bigger difference is in the target, not in the agent. A Kotlin class is final by default, which blocked every subclass proxy in lesson 5, and an agent doesn't care: Advice edits the existing class instead of extending it. The advice's code is copied into the target class, so anything it calls (CallCounts, println) must be reachable from there, in Kotlin as much as in Java.

worked.title: A transformer that never sees its class

steps.say: An engineer attaches an agent to a running test copy of the ticket app, to log the bytes of SeatMap, which loaded at start-up. transform is never called for it. Read the agent and work out why before reading on.
steps.code: public static void agentmain(String args, Instrumentation inst) { inst.addTransformer(new LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap")); // waits for transform(...) to be called for SeatMap: it never is }

alt.html: @JvmStatic fun agentmain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { inst.addTransformer(LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap")) // waits for transform(...) to be called for SeatMap: it never is }

steps.say: A transformer sees class definitions that happen after it's registered. SeatMap was defined an hour ago, and nothing will define it again. To see it, ask the JVM to run the transformers again for that class. That needs three things: Can-Retransform-Classes: true in the manifest, registering the transformer as able to retransform, and the call itself.
steps.code: public static void agentmain(String args, Instrumentation inst) throws Exception { LoggingTransformer t = new LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap"); inst.addTransformer(t, true); // 1. canRetransform = true for (Class<?> c : inst.getAllLoadedClasses()) { if (c.getName().equals("theatre.booking.SeatMap")) { inst.retransformClasses(c); // 2. run the transformers again for it } } }

alt.html: @JvmStatic fun agentmain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { val t = LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap") inst.addTransformer(t, true) // 1. canRetransform = true inst.allLoadedClasses .filter { it.name == "theatre.booking.SeatMap" } .forEach { inst.retransformClasses(it) } // 2. run the transformers again for it }

steps.say: Now transform is called with the class's current bytes and a non-null classBeingRedefined. If it returns changed bytes, they may only change method bodies, the constant pool and attributes. Returning a class with a new field makes retransformClasses throw, and then, as the Javadoc promises, no class was changed. Calls already inside SeatMap methods finish on the old code, and the next calls run the new code.

Byte Buddy packs all of this into the builder. RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION registers the transformer as able to retransform, and retransforms the matching loaded classes. disableClassFormatChanges() stops Byte Buddy from adding members, and Advice changes only method bodies. That's why the lab needs five builder calls and no loop over loaded classes.

lab.title: Count calls on a loaded class, without a restart
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail with NotImplementedError. Read SoundBoard in the test folder: it's a final Kotlin class, and its playAll calls play on this.
Annotate CountingAdvice.enter with @Advice.OnMethodEnter, and its parameter with @Advice.Origin("#t.#m").

Write countCalls(type, method) with the five builder calls from the last section: disableClassFormatChanges(), .with(RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION), .type(`is`(type)), .transform { builder, _, _, _, _ -> builder.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice::class.java).on(named(method))) }, and .installOn(instrumentation()).

Return Installed { transformer.reset(instrumentation(), AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) }. Run the tests until all six pass. Then read the self-call test and compare it with lesson 5's forwarding proxy.
hints: The Gradle test task already passes -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading, so there is no warning. Run a test from an IDE without it, and you'll see the four JEP 451 lines.
If a test counts 0, check that the advice method is @JvmStatic and annotated with @Advice.OnMethodEnter. Byte Buddy quietly ignores an advice class with no annotated methods.
If the uninstall test still counts calls after uninstalling, reset needs the same RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION you installed with.

drill.title: A startup agent from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write a startup agent class whose premain prints its argument string and registers a transformer that prints the name of every class in the theatre/ package as it loads, changing nothing. Then write the one manifest line it needs and the command line that starts it.

answer.html: // manifest: Premain-Class: theatre.agent.LoadLogger // run: java -javaagent:load-logger.jar=verbose -jar show.jar public class LoadLogger { public static void premain(String args, Instrumentation inst) { System.out.println("[agent] args=" + args); inst.addTransformer(new ClassFileTransformer() { @Override public byte[] transform(ClassLoader loader, String className, Class<?> redefined, ProtectionDomain domain, byte[] bytes) { if (className != null && className.startsWith("theatre/")) System.out.println("[agent] " + className); return null; // no change } }); } }

alt.html: // manifest: Premain-Class: theatre.agent.LoadLogger // run: java -javaagent:load-logger.jar=verbose -jar show.jar object LoadLogger { @JvmStatic fun premain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { println("[agent] args=$args") inst.addTransformer(object : ClassFileTransformer { override fun transform( loader: ClassLoader?, className: String?, redefined: Class<*>?, domain: ProtectionDomain?, bytes: ByteArray, ): ByteArray? { if (className?.startsWith("theatre/") == true) println("[agent] $className") return null // no change } }) } }

recap: An agent receives an Instrumentation: through premain with -javaagent (in order, before main), through Launcher-Agent-Class, or through agentmain when a tool attaches to a running JVM.
A ClassFileTransformer sees each class defined after it is registered, and returns new bytes, or null for no change.
retransformClasses changes loaded classes in place: same Class object, statics kept, no initializer run again. Running calls finish on the old code; new calls get the new code.

Since JDK 21 (JEP 451), an agent loaded into a running JVM prints a warning. -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading hides it, -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading blocks it, and the default is meant to become "blocked".
Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder with RETRANSFORMATION, disableClassFormatChanges() and Advice copies code into existing methods, so it sees self-calls and works on final classes.
The limit: retransformation changes method bodies only, never fields, methods, signatures, modifiers or the superclass, and each change reaches every caller in that class loader at once.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate how an agent can add timing to a method of a class that loaded an hour ago, without a restart, what it can't change that way, and why the JVM prints a warning when you do it.
explain.answer: An agent gets an Instrumentation object. It registers a ClassFileTransformer that can retransform, then calls retransformClasses for the loaded class. The JVM hands the transformer the class's current bytes, and the transformer returns new bytes in which the method body starts and ends with timing code. Byte Buddy's Advice does that by copying static enter and exit methods into the body. The JVM swaps the body in place: same Class object, same statics, no initializer run again. So existing objects use the new body on their next call, while calls already running finish on the old one. It can't add or remove fields or methods, or change signatures, modifiers or the superclass, so state such as counters must live in another class. Loading the agent after start-up, through attach or self-attach, prints the JEP 451 warning, because since JDK 21 the JDK wants that ability granted at start-up, with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading or by starting the agent with -javaagent. A future release is meant to block it by default.

deeper.html:
Retransformation and redefinition are two different calls. redefineClasses takes new class bytes that you supply. retransformClasses asks the registered transformers to produce them, starting from the class's original bytes. Both follow the same JVMTI rule about the class's shape, and both need permission in the manifest (Can-Redefine-Classes, Can-Retransform-Classes). Byte Buddy's RedefinitionStrategy.REDEFINITION exists too, but RETRANSFORMATION works better alongside other agents, because each transformer sees the result of the one before it.

Agent order matters when there is more than one. With several -javaagent options, "the premain methods will be called in the order that the agents are specified", and each registered transformer sees the bytes produced by the ones before it. Two agents that both rewrite the same method, for example a monitoring agent and your own, can conflict. Test them together.

This lesson closes the track's "integrity by default" thread: recent JDKs warn before they forbid. Dynamic agents warn since JDK 21 (JEP 451). sun.misc.Unsafe memory access warns since JDK 24 (JEP 498, default --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=warn). Changing final fields through reflection warns since JDK 26 (JEP 500, default --illegal-final-field-mutation=warn). In the runs for this track, none of them had become a hard failure by JDK 27.0.1. To find what will break later, run your test suite once with the stricter settings:

test JVM options for a "what will break later" run:
  --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=deny     (JDK 24 and later)
  --illegal-final-field-mutation=deny      (JDK 26 and later)
  and leave out -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading
